story.headline: Israel vote ends without a majority
story.summary: Israel's Knesset election on Tuesday 27 October has left neither Benjamin Netanyahu's camp nor the opposition with a majority, according to partial results released on Wednesday 28 October.
story.display_body: Israel's Knesset election on Tuesday 27 October has left neither Benjamin Netanyahu's camp nor the opposition with a majority, according to partial results released on Wednesday 28 October. With 76.8% of votes counted, the Central Elections Committee's figures, as reported by the Times of Israel and DW, gave the pro-Netanyahu bloc 54 seats, the anti-Netanyahu bloc led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot 47, and the Arab parties 19. A government needs 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats; Netanyahu's outgoing coalition held 68. Turnout was the highest in decades. The count is not settled: a record of about 650,000 absentee votes, including soldiers' ballots, equivalent to roughly 14 seats, are counted last, and Le Temps says the official result is due on Wednesday 4 November. Netanyahu, whose Likud is the largest party, called for "a strong government of the right" and ruled out relying on Arab parties. Eisenkot, whose Yashar party is second, said voters had rejected Netanyahu and called on him to resign. Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats, urged the opposition to govern in partnership with Arab parties, which several opposition parties have so far refused.
story.why: the Arab parties' gains make them potential kingmakers, and coalition talks that are expected to take weeks will decide whether Netanyahu stays in office and set Israel's course on Gaza, the West Bank and Iran.

story.headline: Trains collide south of Madrid, ten dead
story.summary: At least ten people were killed when two high-speed trains collided at about 08:54 on Wednesday 28 October near Urda, in Toledo province about 150 km south of Madrid.
story.display_body: At least ten people were killed when two high-speed trains collided at about 08:54 on Wednesday 28 October near Urda, in Toledo province about 150 km south of Madrid. The rail infrastructure operator ADIF called it a rear-end collision and suspended the Madrid–Andalusia high-speed line. One train was run by the state operator Renfe and the other by the private operator Iryo. Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, warned that the death toll could rise. She told RTVE that one of the trains may have stopped before the crash; the cause has not been established. Health minister Mónica García warned of "a major tragedy". It is Spain's second major rail disaster this year, after 46 people died in a high-speed collision at Adamuz, in Andalusia, on 18 January. RFI notes that it comes during the campaign for the general election of 29 November.

story.headline: Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil for the US
story.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro, defeated in Brazil's presidential runoff on Sunday 25 October, has left the country for the United States, and Washington says it will grant him a visa.
story.display_body: Flávio Bolsonaro, defeated in Brazil's presidential runoff on Sunday 25 October, has left the country for the United States, and Washington says it will grant him a visa. Argentina's national migration directorate said on Wednesday 28 October that the family crossed the land border into Argentina with valid travel documents and then took a chartered private flight to Guayaquil, Ecuador. A police source told RFI that he had not handed over his passports as a Supreme Court order required, and that they were cancelled as a result; he had said on Monday that he would comply. The senator faces several investigations, one into suspected corruption and money laundering in the financing of a film about his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest after his conviction for attempting a coup. Flávio Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing. Asked about his arrival, Donald Trump said he would approve it and called the election "very strange", without giving evidence. Brazil's electoral court has said that the extension of voting hours, which it granted at both campaigns' request, did not affect the result. His brother Eduardo has lived in Texas since March 2025, having left Brazil to escape its courts himself, Le Monde reports.

story.headline: EU wants Frontex to run deportations
story.summary: The European Commission proposed on Tuesday 27 October to make Frontex, the EU border agency, "the central actor for returns", including helping to deport people from one non-EU country to another.
story.display_body: The European Commission proposed on Tuesday 27 October to make Frontex, the EU border agency, "the central actor for returns", including helping to deport people from one non-EU country to another. Under the draft regulation, Frontex's standing corps would grow gradually to 30,000 officers through a new "European border and return reserve" of 17,000, on top of doubling the agency's own staff. It would get a quick-reaction force that its executive director can deploy at short notice when a member state asks, a centre with an explicit mandate to monitor public social-media content for border risks, and the power to buy equipment, including AI-enabled tools, for member states. Returns from third countries would require an agreement with the country concerned and, the Commission says, respect for fundamental rights. The Commission cites this summer's crisis in Ceuta as a reason; it says irregular crossings have more than halved in two years. The proposal still needs the approval of the European Parliament and the member states.
story.why: Switzerland, as a Schengen associate, takes part in Frontex, and the plan would extend the agency's deportation work beyond EU territory, conditional on deals with the countries concerned.

story.headline: Egyptian court orders Mada Masr shut
story.summary: An Egyptian court on Tuesday 27 October ordered the closure of Mada Masr, one of the country's few remaining independent news sites, after convicting its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah of operating without a licence.
story.display_body: An Egyptian court on Tuesday 27 October ordered the closure of Mada Masr, one of the country's few remaining independent news sites, after convicting its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah of operating without a licence. The court imposed the maximum fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (about $53,400) and ordered the outlet's equipment confiscated. Attalah was detained for several hours and released after the fine was paid; Mada Masr will appeal. Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, who attended the hearing, said the judge refused the defence's requests, appointed a new lawyer for Attalah over her own team's objections and dictated motions on that lawyer's behalf. Attalah also learned that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to one year in prison in a separate "false news" case; a hearing on it is set for 11 November. Founded in 2013, Mada Masr is known for investigating corruption, human rights abuses and the military's powerful role in the country.

story.headline: Attacker shot dead at Israeli embassy in Belgrade
story.summary: A police officer guarding Israel's embassy in Belgrade shot dead a knife-wielding attacker, described as a minor, at about 00:15 on Wednesday 28 October, and Serbia raised its terrorism alert to the highest level.
story.display_body: A police officer guarding Israel's embassy in Belgrade shot dead a knife-wielding attacker, described as a minor, at about 00:15 on Wednesday 28 October, and Serbia raised its terrorism alert to the highest level. Interior minister Ivica Dačić said the attacker had been monitored by the security services as a supporter of the Islamic State group and that the officer, who was slightly wounded, acted in self-defence. Israel's foreign ministry called it an attempted terrorist attack and said no embassy staff were hurt. A crossbow attacker wounded a police officer at the same embassy in June 2024.

story.headline: Cyclone Arnab hits Andhra Pradesh
story.summary: Cyclone Arnab made landfall in India's Andhra Pradesh early on Wednesday 28 October as a "very severe cyclonic storm", with winds of up to 135 km/h, after about 180,000 people were evacuated from Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
story.display_body: Cyclone Arnab made landfall in India's Andhra Pradesh early on Wednesday 28 October as a "very severe cyclonic storm", with winds of up to 135 km/h, after about 180,000 people were evacuated from Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. The India Meteorological Department warned of a storm surge of up to 1.5 m above tide level in low-lying areas. Authorities say more than 12 million people live in the storm's path; trees blocked highways, power was cut, and flights, trains and schools were cancelled. Neighbouring Nepal, still recovering from deadly floods, warned trekkers to stay out of high-altitude areas from Thursday 29 to Saturday 31 October.

story.headline: UBS earns $2.7bn as Credit Suisse merger ends
story.summary: UBS reported a third-quarter net profit of $2.7 billion on Wednesday 28 October, up 8% on a year earlier, and said the Credit Suisse integration will be complete by the end of 2026.
story.display_body: UBS reported a third-quarter net profit of $2.7 billion on Wednesday 28 October, up 8% on a year earlier, and said the Credit Suisse integration will be complete by the end of 2026. Its global wealth-management arm attracted $55.1 billion of net new assets, though total invested assets were almost flat over the quarter because asset management had $5.1 billion of outflows, SRF notes. UBS now expects gross cost savings from the takeover to reach about $13.7 billion by the end of the year, above its earlier target of $13.5 billion; about 90% of the Credit Suisse IT applications in scope are fully shut down. Its full-time workforce fell to 97,593, from 99,085 in the previous quarter. Chief executive Sergio Ermotti said the bank hopes Parliament will settle the new capital requirements "without imposing undue costs" on its shareholders, clients and staff.
story.why: the profit and the job cuts are the backdrop to Parliament's debate on how much extra capital UBS must hold so that taxpayers are not exposed if it fails.

story.headline: Building subsidies to rely on CO2 levy only
story.summary: The Federal Council opened a consultation on Wednesday 28 October on how federal subsidies for energy renovation of buildings will work once they are paid only from the CO2 levy, with the federal general budget no longer topping them up.
story.display_body: The Federal Council opened a consultation on Wednesday 28 October on how federal subsidies for energy renovation of buildings will work once they are paid only from the CO2 levy, with the federal general budget no longer topping them up. Parliament decided this on 20 March 2026 as part of the federal budget-relief programme 2027. The draft revision of the energy ordinance merges the existing Buildings Programme and the energy-law "impulse programme" into one, and caps federal funding at 410 million francs a year until the end of 2034. It concentrates support on replacing fossil-fuel heating with renewables, insulating building envelopes, full renovations and new buildings to the Minergie standard, and tightens eligibility to cut subsidies for work owners would have done anyway. The cantons, which run the programmes, may set stricter rules or add their own money. The consultation runs until 11 February 2027 and the changes are due to take effect on 1 January 2028.
story.why: the reform is a saving, not new climate money; it narrows what homeowners can get funding for.

story.headline: Uber Eats squeezes Swiss bike couriers
story.summary: Food-delivery bike couriers are leaving the Swiss market under pressure from Uber Eats, whose riders are mostly self-employed, SRF reported on Wednesday 28 October.
story.display_body: Food-delivery bike couriers are leaving the Swiss market under pressure from Uber Eats, whose riders are mostly self-employed, SRF reported on Wednesday 28 October. Velogourmet, once Basel's market leader, plans to stop food deliveries within months; its owner Jérôme Thiriet, who also chairs the national bike-couriers' association, said firms paying fair wages "have no chance". Zurich's Dabbavelo closed in 2023 and Smood withdrew in 2026. Just Eat is switching largely to self-employed riders and plans to let go most of its roughly 700 employed couriers, except in French-speaking Switzerland, where a court ruling requires them to remain employees. Unions say the self-employed model avoids social contributions and minimum wages; Uber told SRF that complying with the law is its top priority. Uber Eats riders told SRF they earn about 15 francs an hour on average, with unpaid waits of two to three hours between orders.

story.headline: Swiss–EU statistics pact updated
story.summary: The Swiss–EU joint committee updated the annex of the 2004 bilateral statistics agreement at a meeting in Bern on Tuesday 27 October, with immediate effect.
story.display_body: The Swiss–EU joint committee updated the annex of the 2004 bilateral statistics agreement at a meeting in Bern on Tuesday 27 October, with immediate effect. The changes follow new EU statistics law in areas such as business and foreign-trade statistics, agriculture, social surveys and national accounts; some Swiss tourism and agricultural statistics are no longer produced. The Federal Statistical Office says the update is unrelated to the Bilaterals III package.

story.headline: Moretti joint hearing cancelled
story.summary: Valais prosecutors have cancelled the joint hearing of Jacques and Jessica Moretti, owners of the Le Constellation bar in Crans-Montana, set for Monday 2 November, and will question Jacques Moretti alone.
story.display_body: Valais prosecutors have cancelled the joint hearing of Jacques and Jessica Moretti, owners of the Le Constellation bar in Crans-Montana, set for Monday 2 November, and will question Jacques Moretti alone. He has been in custody since he was accused of violence against his wife, and is undergoing a psychiatric assessment. Citing a psychotherapist's certificate, prosecutors said a confrontation would carry "a real risk of acute psychological decompensation" for her, although her lawyers said she wanted to attend. The investigation concerns the fire at the bar on 1 January; a second confrontation hearing is scheduled for 2 December.

story.headline: Last Laurentide ice cap ended its regrowth
story.summary: The last Laurentide ice cap started a new glaciation, then warming ended it
story.display_body: The Laurentide Ice Sheet, the largest of the ice-age ice sheets, once covered most of North America. Its last surviving fragment is Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island in Arctic Canada. Dating the ice cap's past margins, the team finds it shrank to its smallest size some time after about 3,600 years ago and then began growing again around 2,000 years ago. In glacial terms, that regrowth is the start of the next glaciation, driven by the slow decline in summer sunlight that follows Earth's orbital cycles. The regrowth peaked around 1960 CE. Since then human-driven summer warming has pushed the cap into net mass loss, and the margins are retreating. The authors call this "the termination of the next glaciation", even though orbital forcing is still pushing towards cold. This rests on one ice cap and one paper; the abstract was read via Crossref metadata because the Science page did not load.
story.why: This is direct field evidence that greenhouse warming has already overridden the orbital cooling trend that would otherwise be rebuilding an ice sheet. The question stops being a model projection and becomes something observed in the ice.

story.headline: Chemists isolate stable oxoboranes
story.summary: Chemists isolate oxoboranes, molecules with a boron–oxygen triple bond, after 60 years of trying
story.display_body: Boron is electron-poor and does not readily form triple bonds, so oxoboranes (R–B≡O: a two-connected boron triple-bonded to a lone oxygen) had only been seen in the gas phase, trapped in frozen inert-gas matrices, inferred from reactions, or made as derivatives with weaker bonds. The Würzburg group made three of them by a "remarkably simple" route, and they are stable as crystals at room temperature. Their B–O bonds measure 1.208–1.217 Å, which is exceptionally short and strong. Working independently, a Sichuan-led team used carbon monoxide to trigger a rearrangement and isolated a free oxoborane. X-ray diffraction shows its terminal B≡O unit, and calculations find two perpendicular π bonds, the signature of a real triple bond, though a strongly polarised one. The Sichuan compound reacts with both electron donors and electron acceptors, and the team used that to make neutral and cationic derivatives. Würzburg's press release traces attempts back to at least the early 1960s.
story.why: Two independent groups reaching the same "unisolable" class of molecule in the same week makes the result unusually solid. Main-group chemists now have a new bond type they can bottle and study.

story.headline: Designed proteins make photocatalysis enantioselective
story.summary: Designed proteins turn off-the-shelf photocatalysts into mirror-selective enzymes
story.display_body: Metal polypyridine complexes, which are ruthenium- or iridium-based light absorbers, drive much of modern visible-light chemistry. They cannot, however, choose between the left- and right-handed (enantiomeric) forms of a product, and drug makers usually need only one. The team used generative protein design to build new protein scaffolds that bind these photocatalysts. Directed evolution, rounds of mutation and selection, then turned the protein–catalyst hybrids into highly enantioselective light-driven catalysts. The evolved proteins handle several reaction types, run for many turnovers, can be recycled, and work even with cheap commercial catalyst samples that are a 50/50 mix of both handed forms. Spectroscopy shows the protein lengthens the catalyst's excited-state lifetime and holds the substrate in place, and that positioning is what sets the handedness.
story.why: Asymmetric synthesis has relied on finding the right chiral catalyst. This shows a designed protein can impose handedness on a simple metal complex that no natural enzyme was built to hold.

story.headline: One positron trapped as a quantum cyclotron
story.summary: A single positron is trapped for months as a "quantum cyclotron"
story.display_body: Gerald Gabrielse's group captured one positron (the electron's antimatter twin) from radioactive decay and suspended it in a Penning trap, a container made only of electric and magnetic fields, so it never touches matter and annihilates. In a trap cooled to about 300 millikelvin, the positron's circular motion in the magnetic field falls into discrete quantum levels that can be controlled and read out. This is a "quantum cyclotron", which Northwestern likens to an artificial atom. The positron has stayed trapped for months. The same technique gave the group its record measurement of the electron's magnetic moment. The paper itself is a set-up result: the precise positron measurement has not been made yet.
story.why: The Standard Model requires the electron and positron to have magnetic moments equal in size. CPT symmetry is the rule that predicts this: flip charge, mirror image and time direction together and the laws stay the same. Comparing the two moments at quantum-cyclotron precision would be the strictest test yet of that rule for leptons.

In a trap cooled to about 300 millikelvin, the positron's circular motion in the magnetic field falls into discrete quantum levels that can be controlled and read out. This is a "quantum cyclotron", which Northwestern likens to an artificial atom. The positron has stayed trapped for months. The same technique gave the group its record measurement of the electron's magnetic moment. The paper itself is a set-up result: the precise positron measurement has not been made yet.
fields.why: The Standard Model requires the electron and positron to have magnetic moments equal in size. CPT symmetry is the rule that predicts this: flip charge, mirror image and time direction together and the laws stay the same. Comparing the two moments at quantum-cyclotron precision would be the strictest test yet of that rule for leptons.

story.headline: Trapped ion self-corrects past break-even
story.summary: A trapped ion corrects its own errors without being measured, and beats break-even
story.display_body: Standard quantum error correction repeatedly measures error "syndromes", applies fixes in real time and uses many physical qubits. This experiment does none of those. A logical qubit is stored in several internal spin levels of one trapped ion. Engineered couplings move the disorder each error creates (its entropy) into the ion's vibration, and a second "ancilla" ion cools that vibration away. Errors are dissipated, not detected. Repeating the cycle extended the logical qubit's lifetime past break-even, the point where the protected qubit outlives the best unprotected one. It held both in ordinary lab conditions and under added magnetic noise. The abstract gives no improvement factor. "Break-even" is a threshold, not a margin, and this is one protected qubit, not a computation.
story.why: Measurement and fast feedback are among the most expensive parts of quantum error correction. A route that skips them could make robust quantum memories much cheaper to build.

story.headline: Current spins a helical molecule one way
story.summary: A helical molecule spins one way under electric current, and spinning makes it conduct better
story.display_body: The idea borrows from the Archimedes screw. A helicene, a corkscrew-shaped molecule, was suspended between two electrode tips, and an applied voltage set it cycling with 100% directional preference. Reversing the voltage's polarity reverses the direction. Above a threshold voltage the current through the molecule rises sharply, and stretching or compressing the helix shifts that threshold. Calculations attribute both effects to current-induced torque. The rotation moves from stepwise to continuous, and that lets the molecule pass through highly conducting shapes it cannot reach while at rest. Earlier helical-molecule junctions showed neither effect, which the authors put down to differences in structure and operation.
story.why: This is a prototype molecular motor driven directly by electric current, with perfect one-way rotation and a readout built into its own conductance. Both are prerequisites for molecular machines that a circuit could drive.

story.headline: NMR achieved on a single atom
story.summary: NMR on a single atom, done with a microscope tip
story.display_body: Nuclear spins are well shielded from their surroundings, so they hold quantum information for a long time. The same shielding makes them hard to address. Sander Otte's group used a scanning tunnelling microscope, which images and probes single atoms on a surface, to run nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) on one titanium-47 atom with nuclear spin 5/2. The method is electron–nuclear double resonance: it drives the atom's electron spin and its nuclear spin together. The team resolved the individual nuclear-spin transitions, characterised how the nucleus couples to its electron (the hyperfine and quadrupole interactions), and addressed the nuclear spin even when that coupling was weak. The weak-coupling regime is the one needed for long-lived nuclear-spin storage.
story.why: Nuclear spins can now be addressed one atom at a time on a surface that can be assembled atom by atom. That makes them candidate building blocks for quantum memories made to order.

story.headline: ETH implant burns off blood sugar
story.summary: ETH Zürich implant burns off excess blood sugar with electricity, not insulin
story.display_body: Martin Fussenegger's group in Basel built ECHO, a wirelessly powered implant. Its catalyst is graphite felt studded with gold nanoclusters dusted with platinum, and it oxidises blood glucose into gluconate, which the kidneys excrete. The implant has no cells, enzymes or genetic circuits. A commercial continuous glucose monitor triggers it through a smartphone when sugar runs high and switches it off when levels fall. In diabetic mice, activation at 0.75 V and 10 mA restored normal glucose within an hour. It shifted metabolism towards burning fat, cut body weight and triglycerides, and caused no detectable hypoglycaemia or tissue damage over six weeks (ETH Zürich). All of this is mouse data. No human has been tested.
story.why: This is a Swiss-built, drug-free approach to type 2 diabetes. It removes surplus glucose outright instead of pushing it into fat stores, as insulin does. The open questions are whether it scales to human glucose loads and what long-term implant safety looks like.

story.headline: Cells archive their own RNA for days
story.summary: "Recordanelles" let a cell archive its own RNA for days
story.display_body: Measuring RNA, the readout of which genes are switched on, destroys the cell and captures only the present moment. Randall Platt's Basel group built a synthetic organelle, the "recordanelle", from one engineered protein: a mitochondrial membrane anchor, a module that forms condensates (droplet-like compartments) and a poly(A)-binding protein that grabs messenger RNAs. It can capture chosen engineered RNAs or a sample of up to 90% of the cell's endogenous mRNAs and keep them protected for several days. Short-lived responses, such as interferon signalling or a briefly induced promoter, stay readable in single cells after they have switched off. That means researchers can look back at a cell only once they know it matters, for example a cancer cell that survived treatment (ETH Zürich). The work is in cultured human cells so far.
story.why: Single-cell biology gains a record of what a cell did days earlier, not just a snapshot of the present. That matters most for rare cells, such as drug-resistant clones, which are only identified after the fact.
affiliations: Botnar Research Center for Child Health

story.headline: ALS immunity splits by compartment
story.summary: In ALS, T cells in the spinal fluid track slower disease and those in the blood track faster
story.display_body: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a fatal motor-neuron disease, has increasingly been tied to the immune system. The team used single-cell RNA and T-cell-receptor sequencing, longitudinal immune profiling and imaging flow cytometry on patients' cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood. In the CSF they found long-lived T-cell clones and immune-cell pairs locked in synapse-like contacts, consistent with antigen being presented inside the nervous system. More CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the CSF went with slower progression. More circulating CD4+ effector and regulatory T cells in the blood went with faster progression. In sporadic ALS, cytomegalovirus (CMV)-specific T cells in the CSF and anti-CMV antibodies correlated with faster progression and shorter survival. All of these findings are associations, not proof of cause.
story.why: The immune system appears to have two opposite roles in ALS, protective inside the nervous system and harmful in the blood. Immune therapies may need to target one without suppressing the other. The CMV link is a lead worth testing, not yet a target.

story.headline: Tumour-DNA clearance flags lung-cancer outcomes
story.summary: NeoCOAST-2: clearing tumour DNA from the blood marks lung-cancer patients who stay relapse-free
story.display_body: This sponsor-run phase 2 platform trial treated stage IIA–IIIB non-small-cell lung cancer before surgery. Each arm combined chemotherapy and durvalumab (an anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy) with oleclumab, monalizumab or the antibody–drug conjugate datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd). Two-year event-free survival was 70.5%, 75.7% and 77.9% respectively. Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA, tumour fragments shed into blood) had cleared by the third treatment cycle in 50.9%, 54.5% and 72.5% of patients. Patients whose ctDNA cleared had far fewer events than those whose did not (pooled hazard ratio 0.22). Those with both ctDNA clearance and a pathological complete response (no viable tumour at surgery) did best of all (hazard ratio 0.10 versus neither). Arm sizes were 54–76 patients and not powered for comparison, so the Dato-DXd lead is "numerical", as the authors say.
story.why: A blood test taken partway through treatment could show early which patients need more aggressive follow-up, though prospective trials have to confirm that.

story.headline: Rubin finds its first dwarf-planet candidate
story.summary: Rubin Observatory's first dwarf-planet candidate lies beyond Pluto
story.display_body: Before its 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time has formally begun, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found 2026 ED138. It is a trans-Neptunian object about 46 au from the Sun; Pluto averages 40 au, and 1 au is the Earth–Sun distance. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center announced it on Tuesday 27 October. Matthew Holman (Harvard–Smithsonian CfA) spotted it on 13 October by running Rubin data from March–July 2026 through a moving-object search code. Archival images going back to 2016 pin down more than a decade of its orbit. Its brightness and an assumed reflectivity give a size of 600–1,500 km, large enough that it is probably round. The team says infrared observations are needed to confirm the size and the dwarf-planet status, so the 900 km spread in the estimate is real uncertainty.
story.why: This is the first major Solar System find from the survey that will dominate the coming decade of sky mapping. If the size holds up, it would sit among the largest bodies known beyond Neptune.

story.headline: Dead star hosts a double debris disc
story.summary: A dead star with a double debris disc, shaped by two surviving bodies
story.display_body: All 21 known white dwarfs with gaseous debris discs show the double-peaked emission lines of a single rotating ring. WD J1328−1450 shows four peaks. Spectra from ESO's Very Large Telescope resolve two separate gas rings, one from 0.14 to 0.34 solar radii and one from 0.54 to 1.93 solar radii, with a stable gap between them. The authors propose that each ring is fed by its own surviving planetary body, one a few kilometres across and the other possibly as big as Pluto or the Moon (ESO). No existing model of debris-disc formation predicts this structure. Switzerland is an ESO member state.
story.why: It previews our own Solar System's end state, rocky leftovers grinding down around the Sun's eventual white-dwarf core, and shows that this end state can keep more structure than models assumed.

story.headline: 3I/ATLAS methane is deuterium-rich
story.summary: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS carries methane 13 times richer in deuterium than comet 67P's
story.display_body: JWST's near-infrared spectra of 3I/ATLAS, the third known interstellar object, show methane with a deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio of 3.18 ± 0.30%. That is higher than any methane measured in the Solar System and 13 ± 2 times the value Rosetta found at comet 67P, the only other comet with deuterated methane on record. The detection is a very rare sighting of a deuterated organic molecule in an interstellar object. Heavy deuteration builds up in ices that form very cold under strong cosmic-ray irradiation. The ratio fits the hypothesis that 3I/ATLAS's ices formed in a cold, low-metallicity (poor in heavy elements) interstellar or protostellar cloud, but it does not pin that down. The author list includes the Physikalisch-Meteorologisches Observatorium Davos (PMOD/WRC).
story.why: It is a direct chemical fingerprint of where another planetary system's building blocks formed, and it looks unlike anything that formed around the Sun.

story.headline: Gamma-ray burst shows two origins
story.summary: One gamma-ray burst, two origins: a short burst and a long burst four minutes apart
story.display_body: Gamma-ray bursts are usually sorted into two classes. Short bursts, under two seconds, come from neutron-star mergers. Long bursts come from collapsing massive stars, known as collapsars. Reanalysing archival event GRB 160425A, the team finds two sub-bursts four minutes apart. Nearly every standard diagnostic labels the first a merger-type burst and the second a collapsar-type burst: pulse shape, duration, spectral hardness, shortest variability timescale and the known empirical correlations. The paper reports the mismatch and does not explain it. A single source producing both signatures does not fit either standard picture, so the authors call for the classification scheme and progenitor models to be revisited.
story.why: This adds to evidence that "short = merger, long = collapse" is a rule of thumb rather than physics, which matters for using bursts to find gravitational-wave counterparts.

story.headline: Giant impacts help planets keep air
story.summary: Giant impacts help rocky planets keep, not lose, their primordial atmospheres
story.display_body: A late giant impact heats a planet's interior, which should drive off a primordial hydrogen atmosphere, but it also adds mass, which holds the atmosphere more tightly. This model tracks both effects together. The added mass raises gravitational binding fully. Much of the impact energy does not reach the mantle: melting absorbs it as latent heat, and the impactor's iron core stays superheated deep down. The net result is that impacts push planets towards keeping their atmospheres. In this picture, larger planets with atmospheres are preferentially built by collisions, and smaller planets that missed late impacts lose their atmospheres to starlight. That would imply sub-Neptunes have heavier rocky interiors than super-Earths on average. It is a theoretical result, testable against exoplanet population statistics.
story.why: It offers a formation-history explanation for the gap between super-Earths and sub-Neptunes, one of the clearest features in the exoplanet census.
